topicName: Supervised Learning: Linear and Logistic Regression
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Supervised Learning: Linear and Logistic Regression"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Supervised learning is a foundational paradigm in machine learning where algorithms are trained using labeled datasets. Two of the most essential algorithms in this domain are Linear Regression and Logistic Regression. Despite their names, they serve fundamentally different purposes: Linear Regression predicts continuous numerical values, while Logistic Regression predicts categorical classes."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Linear Regression"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Linear Regression models the relationship between a dependent continuous target variable (y) and one or more independent predictor variables (x). The core assumption is that the relationship can be approximated with a linear equation: y = w*x + b, where w represents the weights (or coefficients) and b represents the bias (or intercept)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Goal: Minimize the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) between the true values and predicted values using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Case: Predicting house prices, stock market trends, or temperature forecasting."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Linear Regression in Python"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following code demonstrates how to implement a simple linear regression model using scikit-learn."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Sample data
X = np.array([[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]])
y = np.array([2, 4, 5, 4, 5])

# Initialize and train model
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

# Make predictions
predictions = model.predict(np.array([[6]])) 
print("Prediction for 6:", predictions[0])"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Logistic Regression"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Despite having 'regression' in its name, Logistic Regression is used for binary and multinomial classification problems. Instead of fitting a straight line, it applies the sigmoid function to map predicted values to probabilities between 0 and 1."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Goal: Maximize the likelihood of the data and apply a threshold (typically 0.5) to map probabilities to discrete classes."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Case: Spam detection, disease diagnosis (malignant vs benign), and customer churn prediction."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Logistic Regression in Python"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here is how you can train a binary classification model using Logistic Regression."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# Sample binary classification data
X = np.array([[1], [2], [3], [8], [9], [10]])
y = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])

# Initialize and train model
clf = LogisticRegression()
clf.fit(X, y)

# Predict class and probability
pred_class = clf.predict(np.array([[7]]))
pred_prob = clf.predict_proba(np.array([[7]]))
print("Predicted Class:", pred_class[0])
print("Prediction Probabilities:", pred_prob[0])"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Key Differences"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Output Type: Linear regression outputs continuous numbers; logistic regression outputs categorical class probabilities."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cost Function: Linear regression uses Mean Squared Error (MSE); logistic regression uses Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss)."},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mastering both algorithms provides a solid foundation for tackling more complex machine learning and deep learning architectures."}]
